report.source_text: Three weeks post-surgery, a significant improvement was noted in the vitreous reaction. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed a whitish scar in the superior and temporal regions of the optic disc, accompanied by a persistent macular star (figure 5). At 6 weeks postoperation, the macula status remained similar to that observed at the third week postoperation, with a reduction in the hard exudates (figure 6). BCVA in the right eye had improved to 6/9, indicating a successful outcome in managing the intracameral gnathostomiasis presenting as neuroretinitis.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A male patient in his 40s presented with a 1-week history of periocular swelling, redness, and decreased vision in the right eye. Initial examination revealed significantly reduced visual acuity (BCVA 6/60 in right eye vs. 6/6 in left eye), elevated intraocular pressure (24 mmHg), anterior chamber inflammation (4+), vitreous inflammation (2+), and fundoscopic findings of fibrous proliferation superior and temporal to the optic disc with peripapillary exudation, hemorrhage, and macular edema confirmed by OCT. A presumptive diagnosis of panuveitis was made and the patient was treated with topical corticosteroids, cycloplegics, and IOP-lowering medication. One week after initial presentation, slit-lamp examination revealed a live nematode in the anterior chamber with whitish material attached to the iris hole. The nematode was surgically removed and sent to the Department of Microbiology, where it was identified as Gnathostoma spinigerum measuring approximately 5 mm in length and 0.5 mm in width, with characteristic morphological features including a typical lip, head bulb, cuticular spines, intestinal tract, cervical sac, and esophagus. Post-operative course showed significant improvement: at 3 weeks post-surgery, vitreous reaction improved with a whitish scar in the superior and temporal regions of the optic disc and persistent macular star; at 6 weeks post-operation, the macula remained stable with reduction in hard exudates, and BCVA in the right eye improved to 6/9, indicating successful management of intracameral gnathostomiasis presenting as neuroretinitis.
